urgent.primary_message: Very high or very low blood sugar can become life-threatening within hours. These signs mean — don't wait.
red_flags: Excessive thirst with fast breathing — may be diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
Fruity or nail-polish breath (typical of DKA)
Severe nausea and vomiting with abdominal pain
Confusion, drowsiness, or difficulty waking up
Low blood sugar — shaking, sweating, confusion that doesn't improve with sugar
A foot or leg that suddenly shows infection or a black patch (diabetic foot)

what_is_it.heading: Diabetes in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Diabetes is what happens when your body can't manage the sugar in your blood properly. Either your pancreas doesn't make enough insulin (Type 1), or your body stops responding to insulin properly (Type 2).
paragraphs: Insulin is a hormone that tells your cells to take sugar (glucose) out of the blood and use it for energy. Without enough insulin — or with cells that ignore it — sugar builds up in the blood and damages blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, and feet over years.

Type 1 usually starts in childhood or young adulthood and requires insulin injections for life. Type 2 — by far the more common — develops in adulthood and is closely linked to weight, diet, family history, and ethnicity. Early Type 2 can sometimes be reversed with diet and weight loss alone.

items.headline: 4.5 million
items.body: South Africans live with diabetes. Roughly half do not know they have it.

items.headline: Type 2 = 90%
items.body: Most diabetes in adults is Type 2 — strongly linked to weight, family history, and diet.

items.headline: Free care
items.body: Diabetes screening, oral medication, and insulin are all free at every government clinic.

items.headline: Reversible early
items.body: Many newly-diagnosed Type 2 patients can return to normal blood sugar with diet, weight loss, and exercise.

pull_quote.text: Every year clinics see patients lose toes, kidneys, and eyesight to diabetes — almost always because the disease was advanced before they were tested. Get tested. It is free.

signs.heading: What you might notice
signs.lede: Diabetes can develop slowly over years (Type 2) or come on within weeks (Type 1). The classic signs are easy to miss — and many people have none at all until complications appear.

items.title: The classic three
items.description: Frequent urination, intense thirst, and unexplained weight loss — especially together, especially over a few weeks.

items.title: Tiredness and slow healing
items.description: Unusual fatigue, blurred vision, cuts and infections that take a long time to heal, frequent yeast or urinary infections.

items.title: Type 1 warning signs
items.description: Sudden weight loss with extreme thirst, especially in children or young adults. Vomiting, deep fast breathing, fruity breath, drowsiness — emergency.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: Diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar.
items.fact: Sugar contributes to weight gain, which is a risk factor. But genetics, body shape, ethnicity, and overall diet matter more than sugar alone.

items.myth: If you don't need insulin, your diabetes isn't serious.
items.fact: Type 2 diabetes causes just as many complications — heart attacks, strokes, blindness, kidney failure, amputations — as Type 1.

items.myth: Diabetics can never eat sugar again.
items.fact: Small amounts of sugar in a balanced meal are usually fine. What matters is the overall pattern of eating, not single foods.

items.myth: If diabetes runs in my family, there's nothing I can do.
items.fact: Lifestyle reduces Type 2 risk by more than 50%, even with a strong family history. Genes load the gun; lifestyle pulls the trigger.

prevention.heading: How to lower your risk
prevention.lede: Prevention is most powerful when started before problems appear. If you have a parent, sibling, or child with Type 2 — your risk is significantly higher and screening matters.

items.title: Healthy weight
items.description: Especially around the waist. Losing 5–10% of body weight cuts Type 2 risk by more than half.

items.title: Move daily
items.description: 30 minutes of moderate activity — walking, cycling, gardening, dancing — most days of the week.

items.title: Plate balance
items.description: Fill half your plate with vegetables, a quarter with lean protein, a quarter with whole grains. Cut sugary drinks first — biggest impact.

items.title: Screen if at risk
items.description: Family history, overweight, age over 40, gestational diabetes history — ask for a finger-prick blood sugar test. Free at every clinic.

items.title: Get tested
items.description: A finger-prick blood sugar test is free at every clinic and many pharmacies. Random reading over 11, or fasting over 7, suggests diabetes.

items.title: If diagnosed, start treatment
items.description: Diet and exercise alone may work for early Type 2. Most people will eventually need oral medication or insulin. All free at government clinics.

items.title: Take medication every day
items.description: Even on days you feel fine. Especially on days you feel fine. Diabetes does its damage silently while sugar is high.

items.title: Check your feet daily
items.description: Diabetes damages the nerves in your feet — you can get serious wounds and not feel them. Look, smell, feel. See a clinic for any sore that does not heal.

items.title: Annual eye and kidney check
items.description: Diabetic eye disease and kidney disease are silent until advanced. Annual checks catch them in time to act.

get_help.heading: Where to start
get_help.lede: Diabetes care in South Africa is free at the point of need. The hard part is starting — once you do, the clinic system can carry a lot of the load.

helplines.description: Every government clinic offers free diabetes screening, medication, and insulin
